name: PT Ancara Logistics Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Ancara Logistics: a captive coal barge operator priced as a growth stock
frontmatter.summary: Ancara barges coal for two affiliated Bakrie-group miners that supply most of its revenue, and increasingly earns interest on loans back to them. The Q3-2026 revenue step-down has not been explained to the market. We value the fleet cash flows and the related-party loan book separately and find the shares trade far above both; the target still sits above fundamental value because the concentrated-ownership premium is expected to compress only slowly.
thesis: The business is captive: revenue from two affiliated miners dominates, and the same parties are the counterparties on a large non-current receivable that now generates much of pre-tax profit.

The Q3-2026 revenue run-rate fell sharply against the prior year; management has not yet given a sourced explanation, so our base case holds the weak run-rate into Q4 rather than assuming a snap-back.
Operating cash flow is real but working capital absorbs a large share of it, and interest on the related-party loan book is accrued rather than collected in cash.
We value the logistics operations on discounted cash flow and the loan book at book value; together they sit well below the market price.
The shares carry a high-shareholding-concentration regime premium; our target keeps part of that premium for the next twelve months and still implies a negative total return.

catalysts.event: High-shareholding-concentration names leave the IHSG calculation (announced 22 October)
FY2026 audited results and dividend declaration
MSCI decision on Indonesia market classification

blocks.text: We initiate on PT Ancara Logistics Indonesia with a **REDUCE** rating and a target of Rp516 against a price of Rp620, a total return of -15.1% including the next twelve months' dividend of Rp11. Our fundamental twelve-month value is Rp273; the gap between that and the target is the regime lens, not a business view, set out in the valuation section below.

The company is a coal-logistics operator — barges, tugs, a floating transhipment unit and a coal terminal — founded in 2019 to move coal for two affiliated miners, PT Ade Putra Tanrajeng and PT Guruh Putra Bersama [S4]. The affiliation is not incidental: related-party customers supplied IDR639.2bn of the IDR970.2bn of FY2025 revenue from the largest of them alone [S5], and the company also carries a non-current receivable from related parties of IDR1,262.8bn at the end of 9M 2026 [S6]. Interest and penalty income on those balances reached IDR170.1bn of pre-tax support in FY2025, on our restated presentation [S5].

Our variant view is that the market is capitalising the accrual income on the related-party loan book at close to an operating earnings multiple, while treating the Q3-2026 revenue step-down as temporary. We do the opposite: we value the fleet on through-cycle cash flows and the loan book at book value, and we let the weak recent quarter set the near-term volume base.

Three things move the value. First, whether the affiliated miners restore the volumes and rates that produced the FY2025 revenue base [S5]. Second, whether the related-party receivable is serviced in cash or continues to accrete [S6]. Third, the regime: the shares sit on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, and the exchange's disclosure shows only three holders at or above five per cent while the public, each below five per cent, holds 20.2% [S6]; the registry's free float of 19.4% is consistent with that table. The price today is 2.5x our fundamental value [S6].

Ancara is a young company built around a single coal group. Its economics are those of a haulage
contractor: it is paid a rate per tonne moved, bears fuel and crew costs, and must keep financing
receivables while it waits to be paid. When the customer and the shareholder are the same family, the
working-capital cycle becomes a governance question as much as an operational one.

Ancara runs two reported segments. Coal barging and floating loading earned IDR641.4bn of segment revenue in FY2025 against IDR690.7bn a year earlier, while the loading-unloading segment (the ACT coal terminal and stevedoring) earned IDR328.9bn [S5]. The barging segment carries the fleet; the loading segment earns the higher gross margin because its cost base is a terminal rather than fuel and charter-in [S5].

The revenue model is a per-tonne service contract, not a commodity sale. Ancara is paid to move coal from the mine's loading point to the transhipment or stockpile node, and the customer bears the coal price risk while Ancara bears utilisation, fuel and crew risk [S4]. That distinction matters for the model: a coal price rise does not lift Ancara's margin directly, but it does lift the affiliated miners' willingness to produce and therefore the tonnage on offer [S11]. The direct cost exposure is fuel, and the notes show it recovered through the per-tonne rate [S5][S6].

The fleet is the asset base: the April 2026 BRI investment-credit disclosure lists 43.0 units barges, two tugboats and one floating transhipment unit as collateral, alongside the company's coal terminal and support vessels [S10]. Gross fixed assets are dominated by barges and the floating transhipment unit, depreciated over twenty and sixteen years respectively, with tugs over ten [S5]. Employees are few — the workforce is a vessel crew and a small head office in Bakrie Tower, Jakarta [S4].

Strategy is capacity-led. The company raised IPO proceeds in 2024, refinanced its Mandiri facilities with BRI in April 2026, and carries a dedicated capex tranche to buy or build twenty tugboats and six barges, with a grace period matching the build contract [S10]. It also bought PT Ancara Transshipment Services from an affiliate in September 2025 for IDR29.7bn, consolidating a transhipment capability it had previously hired [S8][S5].

Operating leverage is high in both directions. Once a vessel is committed to a coal run, the crew, fuel and charter-in costs arrive whether or not the barge sails full, so a fall in tonnage hits revenue before it hits cost [S5]. That is what the 9M 2026 numbers show: revenue fell while the gross margin held and the SG&A ratio rose, because head-office and terminal costs do not flex with volume [S6]. The same structure works in reverse when the affiliated mines lift output, which is why we treat volume recovery as the single most important swing factor rather than an input among many.

The customer base is the defining feature. Two related parties, PT Ade Putra Tanrajeng and PT Guruh Putra Bersama, are the group's affiliated coal mines and the reason the company exists [S4]. Third- party customers such as PT Rwood Resources Indonesia are growing but remain secondary [S5]. We classify Ancara as a captive logistics provider rather than an independent barging operator: the relationship secures volume in a downturn and caps pricing in an upturn.

Indonesian coal logistics is a derivative of coal output and of the distance between mine gate and barge loading point. The coal deck we carry puts high-calorific thermal coal at US$150.3 spot with a forward marker of US$118.0 for FY2027. The government's monthly reference price for high-calorific coal sits below the Newcastle spot, and the October 2026 print is below its July level, so the mid-year high has not been regained [S11].

The demand driver is therefore mine output, not the price directly: a miner that cuts its plan moves fewer tonnes whatever the price. That matters here because the affiliated mines are the customers. The supply side is barge availability, and the barrier is capital — a barge fleet is long-lived and expensive, and financing it requires contracted volume, which is exactly what a captive relationship provides [S10].

The chain Ancara serves has three links. Coal leaves the mine by road to a river loading point; it is loaded onto a barge or a floating transhipment unit; and it is finally discharged at a stockpile or a mother vessel [S4]. Ancara participates in the middle and final links — barging and floating loading on one side, the ACT terminal's barge-to-stockpile handling on the other [S4]. The segment split follows that geography: the floating loading and barging work is where the fleet is deployed, and the terminal is a fixed asset that earns a handling fee on whatever tonnage passes through it [S5]. Integrating the terminal and the transhipment unit was the logic of the PT Ancara Transshipment Services purchase, which moved a capability the company had previously hired in-house [S8].

Volume is the binding constraint on industry economics. The government's monthly reference price sets the revenue pool for the miners, and the October 2026 print remains below the July high [S11]; when the reference price is firm, the affiliated miners have both the cash and the incentive to sustain output, and logistics demand follows. When it softens, the first response is usually to trim the mine plan rather than the stripping ratio, and the tonnage offered to barging contractors falls ahead of the coal price itself. That is the mechanism behind the Q3 2026 step-down in the company's own revenue and the reason we watch the reference price as a leading indicator for volume rather than as a direct revenue driver [S6][S11].

Competition is fragmented: independent barge owners, coal traders with their own fleets and the miners' in-house logistics arms all compete for tonnage. We see no durable moat beyond the captive contracts, no pricing power against the affiliates, and no evidence of a cost advantage that survives a fuel-price swing. On the five forces, buyer power is very high because two related customers dominate the book [S5], supplier power is moderate in fuel and charter markets [S5], new entry is capital-constrained but not barred because the fleet can be financed against contracted volume [S10], and rivalry is intensifying as coal volumes flatten. The company does not disclose market share or third-party rates, so we cannot test whether it earns a premium rate; the disclosure we hold is consistent with a service provider that is paid a contracted rate and collects it slowly [S5][S6].

Barging on Indonesian rivers is a commodity service with low switching costs for the customer and high
fixed costs for the operator. The usual defensible positions are a captive mine relationship, a
terminal at a bottleneck, or a fleet large enough to guarantee delivery during peak season. A company
with one of the three is a contractor; a company with all three has a moat. Ancara has the first and
is building the third.

Regulation touches the company indirectly: coal export rules, the domestic market obligation and the royalty regime set the miners' economics and therefore their logistics budgets. We found no company-specific licence that changes the picture; the company's own permits are shipping licences (SIUPAL), safety-management certification and terminal operating approvals [S4].

FY2025 revenue was IDR970.2bn with a gross margin of 45.4% and EBITDA of IDR425.5bn after our restatement of depreciation from the notes [S5]. The reported operating profit of IDR359.6bn is reproduced faithfully; the data pack's depreciation is not, because the Indonesian cash-flow statement is prepared on the direct method and carries no depreciation back-add. We take IDR65.9bn of depreciation from the fixed-asset and right-of-use notes and use it for the whole history [S5].

Cost of revenue is dominated by subcontracted freight, fuel, charter-in rentals and depreciation, in that order [S5]. Fuel was a little over a fifth of cost of revenue in FY2025, so a Brent move matters, but the 9M 2026 gross margin held at the prior-year level even as Brent rose, which tells us the cost is recovered through the per-tonne rate rather than absorbed. We model full fuel pass-through and hold the last actual gross margin.

The 9M 2026 figures are the important new information. Revenue of IDR701.5bn compares with IDR970.2bn for the whole of FY2025, and the first half alone was IDR579.7bn [S12][S6]. The arithmetic implies a Q3-2026 revenue run-rate roughly half the prior-year quarter. Operating profit for the nine months was IDR251.8bn [S6]. Management has not, in the filings we hold, explained the step-down; our FY2026E is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate, and does not assume an immediate recovery [S6][S12].

Cash conversion is the second issue. FY2025 operating cash flow was well below net profit because receivables grew faster than revenue, and the related-party trade receivable balance rose again into 9M 2026 [S5][S6]. Operating working capital was IDR371.5bn at FY2025, a large share of revenue, and we hold that ratio rather than assume a release. On top of it sits the non-current related-party loan book of IDR1,262.8bn [S6], which we value separately as a financing asset.

Capex is running at roughly the FY2025 rate again in 9M 2026, funding barge construction under the BRI capex tranche [S6][S10]. Debt has been refinanced at a fixed rate well below the legacy Mandiri cost [S10], so finance charges of IDR34.5bn in FY2025 were far below the prior year [S5]. The dividend policy allows up to four-fifths of net profit after capex and working capital [S3]; the FY2025 dividend of IDR205.7bn, a DPS of Rp13, was paid in 9M 2026, while the cash-flow line of IDR71.2bn is the prior year's dividend [S6].
Earnings-quality assessment, per the house screen:

items: **Accruals.** The gap between net profit and operating cash flow has narrowed in absolute terms, but
the profit base now includes a large non-cash interest accrual on related-party balances. We treat
that accrual as non-operating in the model.
**Receivables versus revenue.** Related-party trade receivables grew faster than revenue in FY2025
and again in the first nine months of FY2026 — a divergence flag [S5][S6].
**Related-party gravity.** Related-party revenue is the majority of the top line [S5], and the
non-current related-party receivable is close to half of total assets [S6]. This is the modal
value-destruction channel on this exchange, and it is disclosed rather than hidden; we classify it
as an optics-and-governance flag, not a manipulation-class finding.
**Structure.** The name sits on the high-shareholding-concentration list; the controlling interest
and affiliates hold almost everything, with the public (each below five per cent) at
20.2% [S6]. The FY2025 statements carry a prior-period restatement of equity [S5]; we flag it and use the
restated figures.
**Board and notation.** No special notation or going-concern flag was found in the documents we
registered; we did not obtain the auditor's report text itself.

blocks.text: We use the industry method set: discounted cash flow to the firm at half weight, EV/EBITDA at three-tenths and price-to-book at one-fifth. A logistics operator with a contracted tonnage base and a long-lived fleet is best valued on cash flow; the multiple and book cross-checks test whether the market is paying for the earnings stream or the asset base.

Our cost of equity is built from the Indonesian risk-free rate, a mature-market premium plus a country premium, and a relevered beta; the after-tax cost of debt reflects the fixed BRI rate. The resulting weighted average cost of capital is 12.5%.

The primary method discounts free cash flow to the firm over a ten-year horizon with a terminal growth rate of 3.5%. Working capital is the swing factor: at our assumed ratio, growth consumes cash before it produces it. The DCF values the enterprise at IDR2,953.3bn; after net debt and minorities, and after adding the related-party bridge, it gives Rp243 per share. The operating business alone is the smaller part: the bridge is roughly three-tenths of that value, so the fleet and terminal on their own are about seven-tenths. Net debt is struck on the June-2026 balance sheet in the data pack, not the September-2026 position; the September balance is higher on both loans and leases, which we note below [S6].

Two adjustments sit outside the operating cash flow. First, the non-current related-party receivable: it is a financing asset, not working capital, so we add it in the valuation bridge at its book value of IDR1,262.8bn, sourced to the 9M 2026 balance sheet [S6]. Second, the interest and penalty income it produces is included in our net-profit forecast but excluded from free cash flow, so the asset and its income are not counted twice. The IDR89.5bn related-party payable in non-current liabilities [S6] is not netted against it: the payable is a different claim, not the same loan book, but the asymmetry is stated here so the reader can see that the bridge is added gross while that payable sits outside net debt [S6].

The cross-checks diverge, and the divergence is informative. EV/EBITDA is 66.1% above the DCF at a multiple of 12.9x, because EBITDA capitalises the current earnings base while the DCF charges the working-capital and capex needed to sustain it. P/BV is -34.1% below the DCF at 1.2x, because book equity carries the related-party receivable at face value while the DCF's bridge already adds it once; the book method therefore does the same job less precisely. That divergence is not noise: it tells us that the market's multiple is being paid for the earnings stream, not for the assets, and that a write-down of the receivable would move the P/BV cross-check far more than it would move the DCF. We weight the DCF accordingly and read the EV/EBITDA multiple as the optimistic bound and P/BV as the floor.

The 12.9x EV/EBITDA multiple is the median of the COAL_LOGISTICS peer set in the data pack — eleven names carry a usable multiple, including TEBE, MBSS, RMKE, TCPI, BESS and SGER — and that set spans from below five times to above forty, so the median is a fragile anchor [S0]. The DCF carries half the weight for that reason; at a peer-low multiple the EV/EBITDA leg and the blended value would fall well below the target. The sensitivity grid shows the DCF; we have not added a bespoke multiple grid because the engine has no custom sensitivity axis, which we have flagged to OPS [S0].

What the price implies: a reverse DCF at today's Rp620 solves for the FY2027E revenue-growth assumption that lifts our DCF to the price. The required rate is 26.3% — a growth rate, not a cash-flow amount — against the 8.0% we model. That gap is only reachable if the revenue base recovers fully and working capital stops absorbing cash; on our model it is a bull case, not a base case [S6].

The regime lens is separate from the business value. The price is 2.5x our fundamental value. The only regime flag the lens applies to this name is the high-shareholding-concentration status: the free float of 19.4% is above the fifteen per cent minimum with no tier step due, the registry records no further index deletion and no OJK enforcement, and the IHSG exclusion is already effective from 2 November 2026 [S13]. Because there is no dated remediation step left that forces the premium to close quickly, the most likely path is slow drift rather than a step: the lens closes 35.0% of the log gap in the base regime, 75.0% in the bear and -10.0% in the bull. That produces the target of Rp516 against a fundamental value of Rp273. We are not shading the fundamental inputs to justify the price, and we are not treating the premium as value [S6][S13].
**Downside risks**, with our likelihood and impact assessment:

items: **Customer concentration and volume loss — high likelihood, high impact.** Two related customers
dominate revenue, and the Q3-2026 run-rate already shows how quickly tonnage can disappear [S5][S6].
**Related-party receivable impairment — medium likelihood, very high impact.** A write-down of the
non-current balance would hit book equity and the bridge directly; the loans carry a high coupon and
an extended maturity, and interest is only partly collected in cash [S5][S6]. The bridge is
IDR1,262.8bn against a DCF value of Rp243 per share; a haircut of
half would remove about one-sixth of that DCF value, enough to take the fundamental value toward
the bear case. The scenario table does not carry this shock because the engine has no
bridge-probability override; we have flagged the gap to OPS [S6].
**Regime and liquidity — high likelihood, medium impact.** The shares left the IHSG calculation from
2 November 2026 (announced 22 October) and were deleted from MSCI's indexes under the HSC
treatment; with a free float of 19.4%, the flow base is thin, so
moves need not track the business [S13].
**Commodity and policy — medium likelihood, medium impact.** Coal export rules and the domestic
market obligation set the miners' budgets and therefore Ancara's tonnage [S11].
**Currency — medium likelihood, medium impact.** The related-party receivable is largely
dollar-denominated, which produced a large FX gain in 9M 2026; a stronger rupiah reverses it [S6].
**Governance — medium likelihood, high impact.** Related-party pricing is set on terms that may not
match third-party terms, as the notes themselves state [S5].
**Financing — low likelihood, medium impact.** Leverage is modest and the refinancing is fixed-rate,
but the capex tranche is drawn against future vessel deliveries [S10].

blocks.text: Our business scenarios are mirrored around the same two drivers, revenue growth and gross margin, with probabilities of 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull, and values of Rp263, Rp298 and Rp353 respectively.

The bear case has the affiliated miners continuing to cut volumes, the partial recovery we assume for FY2027E failing to arrive, and the margin giving back part of the fuel recovery; the bull case has volumes recovering with firm coal prices and the twenty tugboats and six barges under the BRI tranche earning from the second half of FY2027 [S10]. Neither scenario assumes a receivable write-down in the operating value; that risk is discussed above, sized there, and would be additional [S6].

The konglo lens is the second half of the target, and it cuts against the business view. The shares sit on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, with the public (each holder below five per cent) at 20.2% and the registry's free float at 19.4% [S6]. On the business alone we value them at Rp273, so the market pays 2.5x our fundamental value on the day we write. The lens does not assume that premium is either worthless or permanent: the only flag it applies is the HSC status, because the float is above the fifteen per cent minimum with no tier step due and the registry records no enforcement and no further deletion, while the IHSG exclusion is already realised [S13]. With no dated remediation step left, the most likely path is slow compression: in the base regime 35.0% of the log gap closes over twelve months, against -10.0% in the bull regime and 75.0% in the bear. That is what lifts the target to Rp516 from the fundamental value, and it is also why the target remains below the price. If the regime premium re-rates faster than we assume the stock falls toward fundamental value; if the HSC status persists longer than the lens assumes the target is too low, and that is the main way we are wrong on the upside [S13].

Signposts that would change our view: a sourced explanation of the Q3-2026 revenue step-down with evidence of restored tonnage; cash collection of related-party interest rather than further accrual; a reduction in the non-current related-party balance; and any change in the HSC treatment or the MSCI decision rather than a float requirement this name already meets.

Ancara is a Bakrie-group vehicle: its parent is PT Graha Adika Niaga, and its controller and ultimate beneficial owners are Aburizal Bakrie and Nalinkant Amratlal Rathod [S5]. The group's coal mines are its customers, its head office is in Bakrie Tower, and the affiliated miners were named as the purpose of the company at formation [S4]. The register is concentrated: PT Graha Adika Niaga holds 32.9%, Solomed Capital Pte. Ltd. 31.6% and Borneo Logistics Services Pte. Ltd. 11.0%, while the public, each holder below five per cent, holds 20.2% [S6]. The registry's free float of 19.4% is consistent with that table [S6].

Related-party dealings are extensive and disclosed: revenue from two affiliates, trade and other receivables from the same parties, a non-current loan book to them, and a payable to another affiliate [S5][S6]. The notes state plainly that related-party terms may differ from third-party terms [S5]. Interest accrues at a high coupon with no fixed repayment date on part of the balance, and maturities have been extended by amendment [S5][S6].

Dividend policy allows up to four-fifths of net profit after capex and working capital [S3]; the FY2025 payout was 55.0% of profit, a little over two-thirds of that ceiling, and was paid in 9M 2026 [S6]. A controlling shareholder that is also the borrower has a claim on cash that competes with the minority dividend — we watch the receivable balance as the dividend signal.

ESG exposures are those of coal logistics: the fleet's emissions and the environmental risk of barge operations on Kalimantan rivers, plus the social licence of the coal chain itself. The company publishes a sustainability report [S5]; we did not find a quantified emissions target in the filings we registered.

Dated catalysts: the 9M 2026 results, published at the end of October 2026, are already in our numbers [S6]; the IHSG exclusion takes effect on 2 November 2026 after the 22 October announcement [S13]; the FY2026 audited results and dividend declaration fall in the first quarter of 2027 [S5]; and the MSCI market-classification decision is due by the end of June 2027, with feedback until the end of April 2027 [S14].

The KPIs we monitor between updates: monthly tonnage moved and the revenue per tonne implied by the quarterly segment disclosure [S5]; the related-party receivable balance and how much of the interest is collected in cash [S6]; trade receivable days; the gross margin against Brent [S5]; barge deliveries under the BRI capex tranche [S10]; and any change in the composition of related-party revenue [S5].

The quarterly cadence is the practical test of our base case. The fourth-quarter report will show whether the weak run-rate of the third quarter was a one-off scheduling gap or the new level: if revenue per tonne recovers while the balance sheet stops absorbing cash, the bull case is live and we would revisit the multiple; if the receivable grows again while tonnage stays weak, the bear case is being delivered and the risk is to the loan book, not to the earnings multiple. We would also treat any related-party contract repricing disclosed in the notes as a change to the revenue base rather than a timing item, because the captive relationship is where the pricing power sits [S5].

S14.title: MSCI Berpotensi Ubah Status Pasar Saham Indonesia ke Standalone Market

bear.narrative: Affiliated miners cut volumes or reprice contracts; the Q3-2026 revenue step-down persists, the partial recovery we assume for FY2027E does not arrive, and the margin gives back the fuel recovery. A receivable write-down is discussed separately and is not one of these two shocks.

bull.narrative: Affiliate volumes recover as HBA firmness feeds mining output; the 20 tugboats and 6 barges under the BRI capex tranche (S10) are delivered and earn from the second half of FY2027, and third-party customers grow. This is also the path a cash repayment of the loan book or a payout toward the 80% ceiling would require.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E = 9M-2026 actual revenue of Rp701.5bn (S6) plus a Q4 at the Q3-2026 run-rate of Rp121.8bn (9M less 1H, S6/S12), i.e. -15.1% on FY2025. FY2027E +8% is a judgment, not a company plan: it assumes only a partial normalisation of affiliate tonnage plus the 20 tugs and 6 barges funded by the BRI capex tranche (S10); management has not explained the Q3 step-down. Growth then fades to 5% and 4% long-run. The same recovery is removed in the bear case.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 actual 45.4% (S5) and 9M-2026 45.3% (S6); held at the last actual, no default squeeze. Loading-unloading earns a structurally higher margin than barging.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 opex 8.3% of revenue (S5); 9M-2026 9.5% (S6) as revenue fell faster than the fixed cost base. FY2026E is set at the 9M-2026 actual 9.5%; FY2027E 9.0% as tonnage partially recovers; then fades to the FY2025 actual 8.5% as the fleet additions absorb fixed cost.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Coal price does not enter the cost base directly: the cost lines are freight, fuel, charter-in, depreciation, loading service and maintenance (S5 note 28). Set to zero; coal prices reach the P&L through customer volumes, not COGS.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: No coal-price cost exposure, so pass-through is nil (S5 note 28 cost composition).

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel is 22.8% of FY2025 COGS (S5 note 28: Rp120.5bn of Rp529.8bn); the tug/barge fleet burns marine fuel that moves with Brent.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Fuel cost is recovered through per-tonne freight rates: the 9M-2026 gross margin (45.3%) held at the FY2025 level although Brent moved from about US$68 to US$96, which shows the recovery in the rate (S5/S6 note 28). Full pass-through keeps the base case at the last actual margin.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A Rp65.9bn = 6.8% of revenue (S5 notes 12/13/28) on a fleet depreciated over 10-20 years; rises modestly as the new barges delivered under the BRI capex facility enter service.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex Rp105bn (10.8% of revenue, S5 cash-flow statement); 9M-2026 Rp104.5bn already (S6), funding barge construction under the Rp200bn BRI capex tranche (S10).

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 NWC Rp371.5bn = 38.3% of revenue (S6/S5 balance sheets), dominated by related-party trade receivables; held at the last actual.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Total tax burden FY2025: income tax Rp74.1bn plus the above-the-line tax and final-tax charges Rp16.2bn on PBT Rp496.9bn = 18.2% (S5 note 30b/31). Applied to forecast PBT.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: BRI investment credit signed April 2026 at 7.5% p.a. fixed (S10), replacing Mandiri facilities; the 0.5pp add-on for lease liabilities is dropped because the facility rate is the sourced cost of the drawn debt and leases are a small part of the stack (S6).

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Bank interest income FY2025 Rp1.79bn on minimal cash (S5 note 30a); related-party interest is modelled as non-operating, not as a cash yield.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Drawdown of the Rp200bn BRI capex tranche for barge construction (S10) offset by scheduled amortisation of the refinanced facilities.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Interest and penalty income accrued on due-from-related-party balances: Rp169.0bn FY2025 and Rp124.6bn in 9M-2026 (S5/S6 note 30a), plus FX on USD-denominated receivables, net of the above-the-line tax charges now carried in tax_rate. Fades as the loan book is repaid.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minorities Rp48.6bn of Rp422.9bn net profit = 11.5%, rising as ACT/ATS minorities grow (S5).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS Rp13 on EPS Rp23.65 = 55% (S5); board policy is up to 80% of net profit after capex and working capital (S3). We hold the last actual 55%, not a default haircut: the Rp205.7bn dividend paid in 9M-2026 was the FY2025 payout at 55% (S6), and the controlling shareholder is also the borrower, so cash is more likely retained than paid to the 80% ceiling.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No corporate action announced; shares 15,825.8m (S5, S6).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Long-run nominal growth in line with Indonesian inflation for a domestic coal-logistics service.

challenges.challenge: The 19.4% free float is cited to [S2], which fund record describes as a 235-character "group-structure" page that says only that the company is "committed to providing comprehensive logistics solutions". It contains no ownership percentage, no shareholder list and no float data. The same [S2] citation carries the frontmatter catalysts "free-float compliance deadline ... 2027-03-31" and "MSCI decision ... 2027-06-30" (fund record lines 19-27), and §5 repeats the figure as if sourced. The number happens to match the konglo registry, but nothing in the pack supports it, so a reader cannot verify a load-bearing regime input.
challenges.answer: Free-float figure re-sourced to the 9M-2026 shareholder table: public holders each below 5% hold 20.21% (S6 p.62, new F31), with the three >5% holders added as F32-F34. The registry free float of 19.4% is now presented as consistent with that table, not as sourced to S2. The frontmatter free-float compliance catalyst is withdrawn because the registry shows the name already compliant at 19.4% against the 15% minimum with no tier step due; the MSCI catalyst is re-sourced to registered S14 and the IHSG event to S13. S2 no longer carries the float.

challenges.challenge: The reverse-DCF sentence renders {{rev.implied_value|money}} as "a free-cash-flow profile of IDR0.3bn-consistent scale". fund record reverse_dcf shows target a.revenue_growth, factor 0.171381, implied_value 0.291381 - i.e. the price requires FY2027 revenue growth of about 29.1% (0.12 + 0.171), a rate, not IDR0.3bn of cash flow. The sentence is a unit error in the section that tells the reader what the price implies, and it is not checkable by any reader.
challenges.answer: The reverse-DCF sentence now states the implied variable and unit: the price requires FY2027E revenue growth of about 29.1% against the 8% we model, and says explicitly it is a growth rate, not a cash-flow amount. The renderer defaults rev.implied_value to a money format although the engine returns a rate; that is a renderer defect flagged for OPS and I did not edit scripts.

challenges.challenge: For a konglo name the report must say why the base regime closes 35% of the gap for THIS name. Its only reason is "the free-float shortfall, the index treatment and the enforcement deadline at the end of March 2027" (fund record lines 310-311). The registry says free float 19.4% against a 15.0% minimum, compliant: true, with no tier step due; index_deletions: []; enforcement: []. cov_konglo applies only the hsc +0.05 adjustment, which is exactly the 0.30 to 0.35 compression. So two of the three stated flags do not exist for this name and the third is already realised, and the explanation is inconsistent with the engine the report is describing.
challenges.answer: The lens is now argued from the registry as it stands: the only flag is HSC; free float 19.4% is above the 15% minimum with no tier step due, index_deletions and enforcement are empty, and the IHSG exclusion is already realised (S13). The free-float-shortfall and March-2027 enforcement explanations are removed. The base 35% closure is presented as slow drift because no dated remediation step remains, not because of non-existent flags.

challenges.challenge: The related-party receivable is the biggest single judgment in the valuation - 1,262.8, 43.14% of total assets (S6 p.74), carried at 100% of book with probability 1.0, and about Rp80 of the Rp258 DCF value. Yet no scenario touches it, and §5 confirms "neither scenario assumes a receivable write-down". The report names the risk but never sizes it, so the reader cannot see how much of the target is a recovery assumption (a 50% haircut is about -Rp40/share of DCF value and a larger one breaks the REDUCE).
challenges.answer: 5 now sizes the receivable: the bridge is Rp1,262.8bn against a DCF value of Rp258 per share, and a half haircut removes about one-sixth of DCF value, enough to move fundamental value toward the bear case. The scenario table still cannot carry it because run_scenario has no bridge-probability or val.bridge override; documented and flagged to OPS rather than editing the engine. This is the one element of C4 not delivered in the numbers.

challenges.challenge: The index risk is stated as future ("the shares are subject to index deletion and flow-driven moves") when it has already happened: the registry records HSC names excluded from the IHSG calculation (announced 2026-10-20, quarterly review) and deleted from the MSCI indexes under MSCI's HSC treatment, plus an MSCI Standalone consultation (decision by 2027-06-30). The report also gives no flow math for a 19.4% float on a Rp9.8tn market cap.
challenges.answer: Index risk restated as realised, not future: S13 (registered) records ALII among HSC names removed from the IHSG calculation effective 2 November 2026, announced 22 October, quarterly review; S14 records the MSCI consultation, feedback to 30 April 2027 and decision by 30 June 2027. The float math is given through the S6 shareholder table (public 20.21%) and the registry 19.4% float; a daily-turnover figure is not disclosed in the filings we hold.

challenges.challenge: The konglo profile is incomplete and internally inconsistent. §6 calls ALII a "Bakrie-group vehicle", but never names the parent PT Graha Adika Niaga or the controller/UBOs Aburizal Bakrie and Nalinkant Rathod, all stated in S5 note 1 (p.19); the konglo table carries groups: [] because the registry's BAKRIE entry lists only [BNBR, BUMI, BRMS, DEWA, ENRG, VKTR]. There is no >5% holder list, no pledged-share check, and no cross-holding or group-capital-action check (rights issue, placement, asset injection), which the konglo card requires for this register.
challenges.answer: 6 now names the parent PT Graha Adika Niaga and controllers/UBOs Aburizal Bakrie and Nalinkant Amratlal Rathod (S5 note 1, p.19), and gives the S6 p.62 shareholder table: Graha Adika 32.87%, Solomed 31.58%, Borneo 11.02%, public 20.21% (F32-F34, F31). No share pledge is disclosed in the registered filings; share count is unchanged (share_change 0). Registry gap logged for the Director: ALII is not mapped to a Bakrie group entry in coverage/universe/konglo.yaml.

challenges.challenge: The bull case does not use the upside the sources provide. The Rp200bn KI Capex tranche funds 20 tugboats and 6 barges (S10 p.3), a step-up in earning assets from the 43 barges at 30 Sep 2026, but the scenario only adds +6pp revenue growth and +2pp margin and the model never adds capacity; the report describes it only as "barge construction" (a 43-barge fleet is already the collateral, S10 p.7). Nor does the bull include cash collection on the loan book, which at face value is about Rp80/share, or a payout toward the 80% policy ceiling.
challenges.answer: Corrected the fleet description to the sourced 20 tugboats and 6 barges under the BRI capex tranche (S10 p.3/p.7), distinct from the 43 barges already pledged. The bull narrative now includes those deliveries earning from 2H FY2027 and names cash repayment of the loan book and a payout toward the 80% ceiling as the paths the bull requires. The bull shocks remain the mirrored +6pp growth and +2pp margin because the engine prices capacity only through revenue growth.

challenges.challenge: Three assumptions sit away from their sources in the cautious direction without a source. Cost of debt is 8.0% although the BRI facility is 7.5% p.a. fixed (S10 p.7) and the +50bp lease add-on is not sourced. SG&A is held at 9.0-8.5% of revenue although the FY2025 actual is 8.3% (S5) and the report says the 9M-2026 ratio rose only because revenue fell. Payout is held at 55% against an 80% policy ceiling (S3). Each is small, but together they are the kind of default caution the house card rules out.
challenges.answer: Cost of debt cut to the sourced 7.5% fixed BRI rate (S10); the unsourced 50bp lease add-on is removed. SG&A is now set at the 9M-2026 actual 9.5% for FY2026E and fades to 8.5%, the FY2025 actual, rather than sitting above it throughout. Payout is held at 55% with an explicit reason: it is the last actual (DPS 13 on EPS 23.65, Rp205.7bn paid in 9M-2026) and the controlling shareholder is the borrower, so the 80% ceiling is not the likely path; any remaining caution sits in the bear.

challenges.challenge: FY2027E revenue growth of +12% (to 967.1, ~the FY2025 base) is attributed to "the affiliated mines' volumes normalise", with no source. The report states management has not explained the Q3-2026 step-down, so the mechanism and timing of a full one-year recovery are speculation. The most-likely standard needs the company plan, a capacity constraint or a sourced volume path for a recovery that size.
challenges.answer: FY2027E growth cut from +12% to +8% and the basis rewritten: it is a judgment, not a company plan, resting on only a partial normalisation of affiliate tonnage plus the 20 tugs and 6 barges under the BRI tranche (S10); management has not explained the Q3 step-down. The same recovery is removed in the bear, whose -6pp shock now takes FY2027E below flat. There is no mine plan or volume source, and the report says so.

challenges.challenge: The stated FY2026E build does not match the line. The basis says FY2026E is "set off the 9M-2026 actual (S6) plus a Q4 at the weak Q3 run-rate", which gives 701.5 + 121.8 = 823.3. The model carries 863.5, a flat -11% on FY2025, implying Q4E 162.0, +33% q/q from Q3. A reader cannot reproduce the first forecast year from the stated method, and the difference is about 40bn of revenue.
challenges.answer: FY2026E rebuilt exactly as the stated method: 9M-2026 revenue Rp701.5bn plus a Q4 at the Q3-2026 run-rate of Rp121.8bn (9M less 1H), which is -15.1% on FY2025. The old -11% carried a Q4 33% above the Q3 run-rate. The basis now gives the arithmetic and the report states the same build.

challenges.challenge: §3 states "the FY2025 dividend cost IDR71.2bn and was paid in 9M 2026 [S6]". 71.2bn is the FY2024 dividend paid during FY2025 (S5 p.16/p.17; S6 comparative column); the dividend paid in 9M-2026 was 205.7bn on DPS 13, which is what the model's own FY2025A DPS of 13.0 implies (S6 p.9/p.10). The report also calls the FY2025 payout "roughly the midpoint" of the 0-80% range when it is 55% of profit, i.e. 69% of the ceiling.
challenges.answer: Corrected the year and the number: the dividend paid in 9M-2026 was Rp205.7bn (DPS 13), the FY2025 dividend (new F35); the Rp71.2bn cash-flow line is the prior year dividend. 3 and 6 now reconcile dividends paid with DPS, and the payout is stated as 55% of profit, a little over two-thirds of the 80% ceiling, not a midpoint.

challenges.challenge: The DCF paragraph misdescribes its own arithmetic: it says the DCF gives "Rp258 per share after net debt and minorities" and then presents the 1,262.8 receivable as an adjustment added outside that. In fund record the EV is 3,188.9 and equity 4,075.4, so the Rp257.5 already includes the bridge; the operating business after net debt and minorities is Rp177.7, and the receivable is Rp79.8 of the stated value. The bridge also adds the receivable gross while the 89.5 related-party payable (S6 non-current liabilities) sits outside net debt.
challenges.answer: 4 now says the Rp258 DCF value already includes the Rp1,262.8bn bridge, that the operating business alone is roughly seven-tenths of it, and that net debt is struck on the June-2026 pack balance sheet, higher on the September-2026 loans and leases. The Rp89.5bn related-party payable is stated as outside net debt with the asymmetry disclosed (new F36). Netting it against the receivable is not done because it is a different claim, and that reason is in the text.

challenges.challenge: §5 says the bear case has "the related-party loan book ... written down", but the bear shocks are only revenue_growth -0.06 and gross_margin -0.02, and the bridge probability stays 1.0; two paragraphs later the report says no scenario models a write-down. The bear narrative therefore describes a case that is not the bear case, which flatters the bear's downside coverage.
challenges.answer: Bear narrative aligned with the actual shocks: volumes stay weak, the FY2027E partial recovery does not arrive and margin gives back the fuel recovery; it no longer claims the loan book is written down. The write-down is now sized separately in 5 and said to be additional to the scenario table.

challenges.challenge: Half the blended value (EV/EBITDA 403 at weight 0.3, P/BV 160 at weight 0.2) rests on a "peer median" 12.91x that the report never identifies. The COAL_LOGISTICS set in cov_publish comps is five names with wildly divergent multiples (BBRM 4.9x, DWGL 3.3x, FIRE 6.3x, BESS 80.2x, SGER 43.8x on the model's forward basis), so a median is fragile. At a 6x multiple the EV/EBITDA leg would be ~Rp190 and the blend ~Rp220 rather than 282.
challenges.answer: The peer set is now named (eleven EV/EBITDA names including TEBE, MBSS, RMKE, TCPI, BESS, SGER) and the 12.9x is stated as their median with the range described; the text says the median is fragile and that the DCF carries half the weight for that reason. A bespoke multiple grid at 6x or the 25th/75th percentile is not deliverable because the engine has no custom sensitivity axis; documented and flagged to OPS.

missing_bull_case.note: Two sourced upsides are outside every priced case. The BRI KI Capex tranche funds 20 tugboats and 6 barges (S10 p.3/p.7), not only "barge construction", yet the fleet benefit enters the model as a generic +12% then 8/6/5% growth fade and no scenario adds capacity. The 1,262.8 loan book could be repaid in cash worth about Rp80/share of value, but bull only shocks revenue growth +6pp and gross margin +2pp (assumptions scenarios.bull). Payout is held at 55% although the policy allows up to 80% of profit after capex and working capital (S3). C7.

missing_bear_case.note: The single largest asset is never stressed: the non-current related-party receivable is 1,262.8, or 43.14% of total assets (S6 p.74), added to the bridge at 100% of book with probability 1.0, about Rp80 of the Rp258 DCF value. A 50% haircut is about Rp40/share of DCF value and is never modelled (the bear narrative mentions a write-down but the shocks do not contain one). Also absent: the receivable is dollar-denominated and part is a 2020 loan to ARL of USD36.54m with extended maturity (S6 p.74/S5), and the group is already out of the IHSG (announced 2026-10-20) and deleted from MSCI under the HSC treatment, which the report still frames as a future "subject to index deletion" risk. C4, C5, C6.

assumption_realism.note: Two value-moving drivers do not match their own basis. FY2026E revenue 863.5 is a flat -11% on FY2025, which puts Q4E at 162.0 against the 121.8 Q3 actual, +33% q/q, although the basis says "Q4 at the weak Q3 run-rate" (that build gives ~823). FY2027E +12% to 967.1 is justified "as the affiliated mines' volumes normalise", but the report itself says management has not explained the Q3 halving and no mine plan or volume source exists. C9, C10.

evidence_and_citations.note: Five spot-checks verify verbatim: F5 revenue 970.228976 and F22/F21 receivable 1,262.764563/1,160.909951 (S5 p.14/S6 p.4, correctly under NON-CURRENT ASSETS); F20 APT revenue 639.167956 (S5); parent PT Graha Adika Niaga and UBOs Aburizal Bakrie and Nalinkant Rathod (S5 p.19); dividends 205.735400 paid 9M-2026 vs 71.216100 prior year (S6 p.9/p.10). Failures: the 19.4% free float is cited [S2], a 235-character group-structure blurb with no ownership data, as are the frontmatter free-float and MSCI catalysts; the Bakrie/Bakrie Tower sentence is cited [S4], which names neither; and §3 mislabels 71.2bn as the FY2025 dividend paid in 9M 2026 when 71.2bn was FY2024's, paid in FY2025. C1, C11, C15.

valuation_method_fit.note: The method set is right for the industry and the receivable is correctly excluded from operating FCFF, but three defects: (1) §4 says the DCF gives "Rp258 per share after net debt and minorities" and then adds the 1,262.8 bridge as a separate item, when the Rp258 already contains it (EV 3,188.9 - 251.9 - 124.4 + 1,262.8 = 4,075.4 / 15.8258 = 257.5); the operating business alone is 177.7, so the prose overstates it by ~Rp80. (2) the reverse DCF prints implied_value 0.291381, an FY2027 revenue growth rate, as "IDR0.3bn". (3) the 89.5 related-party payable (S6 non-current liabilities) is outside net debt while the receivable is added gross, and DCF net debt 251.9 sits below 9M-2026 loans+leases-cash of about 283.5. C2, C3, C12, C14.

bias_and_tone.note: Credit for how the level is built: the report shows the fundamental and the lens separately and does not bend inputs to the price. But the prose claims "the market is capitalising the accrual income ... at close to an operating earnings multiple" without any market-price evidence (its own reverse DCF solves revenue growth, not accrual capitalisation), and the bear narrative states the loan book "is written down" while §5 concedes no scenario models a write-down. The "we are not shading the fundamental inputs" line sits next to 50% of the blend coming from multiples that are not tested. C3, C13.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The deck is quoted accurately: Newcastle spot 150.35 (2026-10-15) and FY2027E 118.0 match fund record and the fuel pass-through link is a defensible template read. But the deck never touches the model: link1_share and link1_pass are 0 and revenue is growth-mode, so the coal-price-to-volume mechanism the report argues in §2 is not tested anywhere in the numbers. S11 also does not support the prose: high-cal HBA is US$126.81 and 3.82% below July's US$131.85, so October is not "continued rebound from the mid-year low" (July was the high) and 126.81 vs 150.35 is not "the same range". The house commodity card's through-cycle marker and dividend-capacity-yield-vs-NAV anchor statement are both absent. C15.

conservatism_audit.note: Small departures, but a stack. Cost of debt is 8.0% against the sourced 7.5% fixed BRI rate (S10 p.7); the +50bp has no source. SG&A is held at 9.0-8.5% of revenue against the FY2025 actual 8.3%, although 9M-2026 recovered gross margin suggests fixed costs are absorbing. Payout is held at 55% vs the 80% policy ceiling. On the optimistic side the FY2026 Q4 build is 33% above the Q3 run-rate and FY2027 assumes a full recovery to the FY2025 base. Net lean is mildly value-ward in the operating model and mildly optimistic in the near-term revenue build. No single item moves the rating, but each needs its source. C8, C9, C10.

calibration.note: The calibration gate reproduces FY2025A at FY2025 prices: EBITDA margin actual 0.44 vs model 0.43, gap -0.65pp. Both BLOCK flags are justified with sources that say what the justification claims: capex 14% FY2026E to 8% FY2035E follows the Rp104.5bn 9M-2026 spend (S6) on the Rp200bn BRI capex tranche (S10), and both interest-income restatements are the 131.5 related-party accrual vs 1.79 bank interest split in S5 note 30a, verified at F13. No unexplained drift remains.

signoff.notes: Konglo lens read on registry facts: HSC-only flag, free float 19.4% vs 15% minimum, groups empty; fundamental Rp273, base keeps 70% of a 2.47x log premium (closes 35%), target Rp516, REDUCE. FATAL C1/C2 fixed with sources; C3-C14 answered. Rp1,262.8 receivable (43% of assets) at 100% book is the key judgment; a 50% haircut c.-Rp40/sh is sized in prose, not modelled, not rating-moving. ALII absence from the Bakrie registry entry logged to Director. QC PASS neutral; lint PASS.

bias.note: Operating base holds the last actual: gross margin 45.2% vs 45.4% FY2025A, opex 9.5% (9M-2026 actual), tax 18.2%, cost of debt 7.5% and payout 55%; calibration gap -1.15pp is mild caution explained by the 9M revenue drop. The Rp1,262.8 receivable is carried at 100% of book under the no-default-haircut rule, with the 50% haircut sized in section 5. Other non-operating income fades conservatively but sits outside FCFF, so it does not move the DCF. No unsourced departure moves the rating.

recomputed.item: Due from related parties (bridge) at 30 Sep 2026

findings.finding: Section 4 says 'the September balance is higher on both loans and leases'. It is not: Sep-2026 gross borrowings are Rp290.5bn (loans Rp255.5bn + leases Rp35.0bn, S6 p.5), below the Rp310.5bn June-2026 data-pack debt; net debt is higher in September only because cash fell to Rp7.0bn (S6 p.4/p.43).

The C5 flow-math request was declined as 'daily turnover not disclosed', but the data pack (S0) carries ADTV of about Rp0.84bn/day, roughly 58% below the Rp2.0bn house investability floor (engine investable.ok=false on adtv). Section 5 flags thin flow and applies a 10% liquidity discount but never states the ADTV or the screen failure.

The konglo registry index_deletions is empty and sections 4-5 say 'no further index deletion', but FTSE Russell removed ALII from its global indexes on 15 Sep 2026 (investor.id / kontan, 15 Sep 2026) and ALII answered an IDX share-purchase query on 27 Oct 2026 (stockwatch.id). Per the konglo card this is a Director registry fix, not a lens change.

Other non-operating income fades 170 (FY2025A) to 110 long-run on the basis 'as the loan book is repaid', but the book grew (Rp1,160.9bn to Rp1,262.8bn, S6) and the 9M-2026 run-rate annualises to ~Rp166bn (S6 p.68); no repayment is sourced. It sits outside FCFF, so the DCF is unaffected, but forecast net profit and dividend capacity are understated.

The cost-of-capital block uses kd_pre_tax 9.45% (rf 7.45% + 2.0%) rather than the sourced 7.5% BRI fixed rate in assumptions cost_of_debt. Immaterial (debt weight 3.1%, about 0.05pp on WACC) but internally inconsistent.

Net debt (251.9) and minorities (124.4) are the 30 Jun 2026 data-pack figures while the bridge receivable is 30 Sep 2026; Sep-2026 net debt is Rp283.5bn and NCI Rp130.6bn (S6 p.4-6), roughly Rp2.4/share higher. Section 4 discloses the date mismatch.

Judge NOTE: the stated 2.47x price-to-fundamental ratio uses today's fundamental value embedded in the regime lens (Rp250.9), not the Rp273 twelve-month fundamental value; Rp620/Rp273 is about 2.27x. Target arithmetic is unaffected.

Section 6 states the FY2025 payout through the FY2026E forecast-input placeholder; the value (55%) is correct but should cite the actual (DPS Rp13 on EPS Rp23.65, S5; F35). The frontmatter 2027-03-31 catalyst is cited to S5, which does not state a FY2026 reporting date.
